coach_says: Qxd5+ gives your queen away for a pawn: the d5 pawn is guarded by the white queen on b3 along the b3-c4-d5 diagonal, so Qxd5 simply wins your queen. The check made it feel forcing, but before capturing always ask what is guarding the piece you take. Quiet moves like Ra6 or Nf5, building up against d5 and covering b7, kept the game level.
concept: capturing a defended pawn with the queen

coach_says: Your knight on f3 is pinned to the queen by Bg4, and d3 does nothing about it. Black jumps Nd4, piling onto the pinned knight, and after Nxf3+ gxf3 Bh3 your kingside is wrecked and the rook on f1 is attacked, so you lose the exchange. Take the d4 square away with c3 (or ask the bishop the question with h3 first) before the knight lands there.

Against a queen, a c-pawn on the seventh is a draw because of a stalemate trick: run your king to the a8 corner, and if Black ever takes the c7 pawn it is stalemate. Kc8 walks away from the corner, and Black's king comes up with Ke6 so that after Kd8 Qd7 is mate. Ka8 (or Ka7) keeps the draw.

Your bishop was already doing a great job on f6, and Be5 puts it where White's f-pawn kicks it with f4, gaining a tempo and tidying up White's broken kingside. You are still better, but you gave White a free useful move. Moves like a4, chasing the b3 bishop, or bringing the queen towards White's open king (Qd7, Qd6) keep the pressure up instead.

When Black plays ...d5 hitting your e4 pawn, the most active answer is to take it with exd5: then Black's own e5 pawn is the one under pressure. Nc3 just defends, and Black can push ...d4, kicking your knight back with tempo and grabbing space. In gambit openings, accept the pawn when it also opens lines for you.

You were already a pawn up; Bxc2 grabs a second one but sends your bishop deep into White's camp where nothing protects it. After Bd7+ Kb8 Ba4 the bishop on c2 is attacked and you have to give material back to save it, and the extra pawn disappears. Before grabbing with a piece, check whether it can be hit after a check; here Bg6 keeps the pawn and a safe, active bishop.
also: checks gain tempo on loose pieces

coach_says: White's king is still in the centre and the queenside pawns are loose, so strike at once with a5. If bxa5 the bishop on b2 is left hanging to Qxb2, and otherwise you open the a-file against White's undeveloped pieces. Bd7 is a slow developing move that gives White time for Bd3, trading off your strong knight on f5.
concept: undermine the b4 pawn with a5

coach_says: Count attackers and defenders on d4 before recapturing: Black hits it with Nc6, Nf5 and the queen on b6, three pieces, and you only defend with Nf3 and the queen. After cxd4 Black wins that pawn. Bd3 first, offering to trade off the f5 knight, removes one attacker so you can recapture safely.

White's h-pawn is the one that can run, and right now it is unprotected. Rh5 attacks it straight away and keeps the game level. After c5, White plays h4 and the pawn gets support, so your rook ends up chasing it while the bishops check your king. In rook against bishops endings, go after the passed pawn before it gets moving.

Your rook on d3 was attacked, but Rd4 just chases the bishop to a better square and leaves c2 unguarded. Rd2 guards c2 and heads for d7, where the b5 bishop supports it, and from there the rook hits f7 and wins back your pawn. Look for ways to get a rook onto the seventh rank when the enemy pawns are still at home.
f6 is fine: it kicks the strong e5 knight and the position stays balanced. Nd6 was an equally good choice.

There is nothing to choose here: whichever way you recapture, the knight on d5 takes your bishop on f4. The mistake came earlier with Nd6+, which gave away a piece because the f4 bishop was already loose.
Kxe7 is right: take the dangerous passed pawn at once.
The position is lost whatever you play; Black's pawns are too strong for the lone bishop. Be6 changes nothing.
Kb3 is as good as anything in a lost position; the king stays near Black's queenside pawns.
Bxd3 is the best move: trading off White's attacking bishop keeps your extra pawn and a safe position.

Your back rank is weak: the king on h8 has no escape square, and Rxc5 takes one of your two rooks off it. Now Qf7 threatens Qf8+ Rxf8 Rxf8 mate, and you have to go back with Rcc8 while the e-pawn races up. Rf8, challenging White's rook on the f-file, was the way to stay safe before grabbing pawns.
